summary.text: Bethany was a village on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about fifteen stadia (roughly 2.8 km) from Jerusalem, where the mount begins its descent toward the Judean Desert. It lay in Judea, which after Herod the Great's death was ruled by his son Archelaus and then by Roman governors. The Gospel of John identifies it as the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary and the place where Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead.

history.text: John says Lazarus had been "in the tomb four days already" when Jesus arrived, and describes the tomb as "a cave, and a stone lay against it." Mark and Matthew describe a meal at Bethany in the house of "Simon the leper," where a woman broke an alabaster jar of costly ointment and poured it over Jesus' head. The Gospels say Jesus stayed at Bethany during his last days in Jerusalem, and Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus leading his disciples "out as far as Bethany" and blessing them.

By the Byzantine period the village's original name had been replaced with one recalling Lazarus, and a memorial church complex, the Lazarium, was built near his tomb in the fourth century. It was destroyed and rebuilt more than once over the following centuries, and the tomb as it appears today dates from the medieval period, with an entrance from the sixteenth century.

Today the site is the Palestinian town of al-Eizariya, whose Arabic name preserves the memory of Lazarus ("al-Azir"). A Franciscan church, consecrated in 1954 over the remains of three earlier churches, stands about 50 meters from the traditional Tomb of Lazarus, which visitors enter by a stairway from an entrance beside a mosque.

scripture.textWEB: He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, and camped there.
Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,
When they came near to Jerusalem, to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples
Jesus entered into the temple in Jerusalem. When he had looked around at everything, it being now evening, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
The next day, when they had come out from Bethany, he was hungry.

While he was at Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at the table, a woman came having an alabaster jar of ointment of pure nard—very costly. She broke the jar and poured it over his head.
When he came near to Bethsphage and Bethany, at the mountain that is called Olivet, he sent two of his disciples,
He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands and blessed them.
Now a certain man was sick, Lazarus from Bethany, of the village of Mary and her sister, Martha.
So when Jesus came, he found that he had been in the tomb four days already.
Jesus therefore, again groaning in himself, came to the tomb. Now it was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
Now Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away.
Then, six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, who had been dead, whom he raised from the dead.
Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let’s go into Judea again.”

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
